nameStory: The four-spotted skimmer gets its straightforward name from the four dark wing spots that stand out like tiny ink blots on its transparent wings. These distinctive spots make it one of the easiest dragonflies to identify, earning it the nickname 'four-spot' among dragonfly enthusiasts.
description: The four-spotted skimmer is a medium-sized dragonfly with a golden-brown body and four prominent dark spots decorating its clear wings - one spot near the tip of each wing. These sturdy dragonflies are excellent fliers that patrol ponds, lakes, and slow streams throughout New England from late spring through early fall. Adults typically measure about 1.7 inches long with a wingspan reaching nearly 3 inches, making them substantial enough to easily spot from a distance.

idTips.label: Wing spots
idTips.description: Four distinct dark brown or black spots, one located near the tip of each wing, stand out clearly against the otherwise transparent wings like bold punctuation marks

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Golden-brown to amber-colored body that feels warm to the touch and has a slightly waxy texture when handled gently

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Hovers and darts with quick, purposeful movements, often returning to the same perching spot on a reed or branch that feels slightly bent under their weight

idTips.label: Wing base
idTips.description: Small amber or yellowish patches at the base of the hindwings that catch sunlight like tiny stained glass windows

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Frequently lands on vegetation tips or bare branches that sway slightly, holding wings perpendicular to their body in classic dragonfly fashion

habitat: Four-spotted skimmers prefer shallow, weedy ponds, lake edges, marshes, and slow-moving streams with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They're commonly found around beaver ponds, farm ponds, and woodland pools where the water warms quickly in spring sunshine. These adaptable dragonflies thrive from sea level to mountain elevations throughout New England's diverse wetland habitats.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in mid to late May, with peak emergence occurring in early June when you'll see their shed larval skins clinging to cattails and other pond vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August when adults are most visible patrolling their territories, mating, and laying eggs in shallow water among aquatic plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early September, though numbers decline significantly by late August as the breeding season winds down.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; larvae spend two full years developing underwater before emerging as adults, surviving ice-covered ponds in the muddy bottom sediments.

funFact: The four-spotted skimmer is Alaska's official state insect - quite remarkable for a dragonfly, since most people think of Alaska as too cold for these sun-loving creatures, yet they thrive in the brief but intense Arctic summer!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the twelve-spotted skimmer, but remember the simple math: four-spotted skimmers have four dark wing spots total while twelve-spotted skimmers are covered in multiple light and dark spots. If you count four spots and stop, you've found your four-spotted friend!
contextualKnowledge: In Europe, this same species is called the 'four-spotted chaser' rather than skimmer, reflecting different regional naming traditions for dragonflies. The terms 'chaser' and 'skimmer' refer to similar hunting behaviors but developed independently on different continents.
compareHints: Among its skimmer relatives, the four-spotted is distinguished by having the fewest and most clearly defined wing markings - just four bold spots compared to the twelve-spotted skimmer's busy pattern or the widow skimmer's broad white patches. The golden-winged skimmer has amber throughout its wings rather than distinct spots, while the great blue skimmer lacks prominent wing markings entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Libellula cousins, the widow skimmer's wing bands are by far the boldest and most extensive - twelve-spotted skimmers have distinct spots rather than bands, while slaty skimmers lack the dramatic black markings entirely.

Among New England's skimmer species, mature male Slaty Skimmers are distinguished by their uniform slate-blue coloration, unlike the bold white patches of Widow Skimmers or the spotted wings of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.

Among its Libellula relatives, twelve-spotted skimmer is unique in having exactly three spots per wing - four-spotted has one large spot per wing, while widow skimmer has broad dark bands rather than distinct spots.

Among New England's Libellula skimmers, male Spangled Skimmers are the only ones with solid metallic blue coloring - Great Blue Skimmers have blue abdomens but different thorax colors, while Slaty Skimmers are more gray-blue.

Among its Libellula cousins, the Painted Skimmer is unique for having amber coloring at both wing bases AND tips - the Twelve-spotted has clear wings with dark spots, the Widow Skimmer has dark bases but clear tips, and the Four-spotted has amber only at the wing bases.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Great Blue Skimmer stands out for its large size and solid blue coloration without distinctive wing patterns.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Golden-winged Skimmer's amber wing patches set it apart from most relatives.
Among its Libellula relatives, Needham's Skimmer is distinguished by having dark wing bases without the white patches of Widow Skimmers or the multiple spots of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.
